name: Logarithms
intro: **When stuck, go back to the definition.** log_a b = c means a^c = b, and rewriting in exponential form settles most doubts in one line (§1).
Check the domain before you celebrate a root: the argument of every log must be positive and the base must be positive and ≠ 1. Extraneous roots are the main source of lost marks here.

qs.q: Find the value of log₂ 64.
qs.h: §1 — ask what power of 2 gives 64.

qs.q: log₃ (1/81) equals
qs.h: §1 — a reciprocal argument gives a negative log.

qs.q: If log_x 27 = 3, find x.
qs.h: §1 — rewrite as x³ = 27. The unknown is the base here, not the argument.

qs.q: log₈ 32 equals
qs.h: §2 — put both numbers on base 2 and take the ratio of the exponents.

qs.q: Find the value of log₅ 125 + log₂ 32.
qs.h: §1 — evaluate each term separately; the bases differ, so no law applies across them.

qs.q: If log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, then log₁₀ 5 equals
qs.h: §3 — 5 = 10/2, so use the quotient law.

qs.q: Find the value of log₁₀ 8 + log₁₀ 125.
qs.h: §2 — the product law. 8 × 125 is deliberately a power of 10.

qs.q: log₁₀ 45 − log₁₀ 9 + log₁₀ 2 equals
qs.h: §2 — combine into a single log of one fraction before evaluating.

qs.q: If log₂ x = 5, find log₈ x (as a fraction).
qs.h: §2, change of base — log₈ x = log₂x / log₂8.

qs.q: The value of log₂ 3 × log₃ 4 × log₄ 8 is
qs.h: §2 — a chain of change-of-base factors telescopes: the intermediate bases cancel.

qs.q: Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010 and log₁₀ 3 = 0.4771, find log₁₀ 12 to four decimal places.
qs.h: §2 — factorise 12 as 2² × 3, then use the product and power laws.

qs.q: If log_a b = 3, then log_b a equals
qs.h: §2 — swapping base and argument takes the reciprocal, not the negative.

qs.q: Solve (log₂ x)² − 3 log₂ x + 2 = 0 and give the sum of the roots in x.
qs.h: §4 — substitute t = log₂ x, solve for t, then convert back. The question asks for x, not t.
qs.s: t² − 3t + 2 = 0 ⟹ t = 1 or 2 ⟹ x = 2 or 4 ⟹ sum = 6. (Answering 3 gives the sum of the t values.)

qs.q: If (log₁₀ x)² − 5 log₁₀ x + 6 = 0, the product of the roots in x is
qs.h: §4 — the roots in x multiply to 10^(sum of the t values).

qs.q: Solve log₃ x + log_x 3 = 2. Find x.
qs.h: §4 — the second term is the reciprocal of the first, so set t = log₃ x and use t + 1/t.

qs.q: If log₂ x + log_x 2 = 5/2, the possible values of x are
qs.h: §4 — t + 1/t = 5/2 gives two reciprocal values of t, and both are valid here.
qs.s: t = 2 or ½ ⟹ x = 2² or 2^½ ⟹ 4 and √2.

qs.q: If (log₅ x)² = log₅ x + 2, find the sum of all values of x.
qs.h: §4 — t² − t − 2 = 0. A negative value of t is perfectly legal; it gives a fractional x.

sets.name: Nested logs, domains and extraneous roots

qs.q: Solve log₂(log₃(log₄ x)) = 0. Find x.
qs.h: §5 — peel one layer at a time from the outside in. Remember log_a 1 = 0.

qs.q: If log₃(log₂ x) = 1, then x is
qs.h: §5 — two layers only.

qs.q: Solve log₂(x² − 3x + 4) = 1 and give the sum of the roots.
qs.h: §5 — convert to exponential form, then check that both roots keep the argument positive.
qs.s: x² − 3x + 4 = 2 ⟹ x² − 3x + 2 = 0 ⟹ x = 1 or 2 ⟹ sum = 3. Both are valid (the argument equals 2 in each case).

qs.q: The number of real solutions of log₁₀(x − 1) + log₁₀(x + 1) = log₁₀ 8 is
qs.h: §6 — combine, solve, then apply the domain condition x > 1. One algebraic root does not survive.
qs.s: x² − 1 = 8 ⟹ x = ±3, but x = −3 makes log(x − 1) undefined ⟹ 1 solution (x = 3).

qs.q: Solve log₄(x + 3) − log₄(x − 1) = 1. Find x (as a fraction).
qs.h: §5 — the quotient law, then convert. Check x > 1 at the end.

qs.q: The solution set of log₂ x > 3 is
qs.h: §7 — a base greater than 1 preserves the direction of the inequality.

qs.q: How many digits does 2¹⁰⁰ have? (Take log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010.)
qs.h: §3 — the number of digits is ⌊n log₁₀ 2⌋ + 1.

qs.q: The solution set of log_(1/2) x > 2 is
qs.h: §7 — a base between 0 and 1 flips the inequality. Don't forget x > 0.
qs.s: x < (½)² = ¼ together with x > 0 ⟹ 0 < x < 1/4.

qs.q: Find the number of digits in 3⁵⁰. (Take log₁₀ 3 = 0.4771.)
qs.h: §3 — same rule as E2.

qs.q: The characteristic of log₁₀ 0.00456 is
qs.h: §3 — write the number in scientific notation; the power of 10 is the characteristic.

qs.q: Find log₉ 27.
qs.h: Put both on base 3.

qs.q: If log₁₀ x = 2.5, then x equals
Simplify log₂ 8 + log₃ 9 − log₅ 25.
qs.h: Evaluate each term on its own base.

qs.q: The value of log₂ 5 × log₅ 8 is
qs.h: The chain collapses.

qs.q: Solve log₃(x − 2) = 2. Find x.
qs.h: Convert to exponential form.

qs.q: Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, the number of digits in 2⁶⁴ is
qs.h: Floor plus one.

qs.q: If (log₂ x)² − 4 log₂ x + 3 = 0, find the product of the roots in x.
qs.h: Solve in t, then convert.

qs.q: The value of 1/log₂ 30 + 1/log₃ 30 + 1/log₅ 30 is
qs.h: Each reciprocal is a log to base 30; then use the product law.

qs.q: Solve log₅(x + 1) + log₅(x − 3) = 1. Find x.
qs.h: Combine, solve, then discard whatever breaks the domain.
qs.s: (x + 1)(x − 3) = 5 ⟹ x² − 2x − 8 = 0 ⟹ x = 4 or −2; only x = 4 satisfies x > 3.

qs.q: If a, b, c are in GP, then log a, log b, log c are in
qs.h: §8 — taking logs turns multiplication into addition.
qs.s: b² = ac ⟹ 2 log b = log a + log c ⟹ the logs are in AP.

audit: A2, A3
solving for the argument when the base is the unknown, or missing the sign on a reciprocal argument (§1)
not converting to a common base before combining (§2)
applying a law across logs with different bases, which is not permitted
B6
negating instead of reciprocating when base and argument swap
reporting the answer in t when the question asks for x (§4)
C3, C4
missing the second reciprocal root of t + 1/t = k
D1, D2
peeling the nested logs from the inside out instead of the outside in (§5)
D4, M9
keeping an algebraic root that violates the domain (§6)
E1, E3
not flipping the inequality when the base lies between 0 and 1 (§7)
forgetting the +1 in the digit-count rule (§3)
E5
reading the characteristic of a number below 1 as one unit too negative
not recognising that logs convert a GP into an AP (§8)
